extracted.intended_audience: physicians, surgeons, natural philosophers, and Royal Society contributors (late 17th-century scientific readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for conducting, recording, and judging observational/experimental natural-history and medical trials (animal experiments, surgical trials, and rain-gauging) as presented in 17th-century Royal Society communications. Emphasis on experimental setup, choice of models, measurement technique, and observation of outcomes and adverse effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human outcome as the standard for therapeutic efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “since the only standard of their use is their success on the human body”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard: the ultimate test of a styptic (or other medical remedy) is its success in humans. Therefore experiments on animals must be designed and interpreted with human outcomes as the benchmark rather than animal-only results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose animal models proportional in size and age to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: “we ought to make our experiments on those animals whose size and age bear a proportion to it: for nothing is more obvious in wounding the arteries of living animals, than that the protrusion of their blood bears a proportion to their bulk: and in dissection, the arteries of the foetus are remarkably thinner than those of an adult: but those of aged bodies grow still thicker, and frequently become cartilaginous, and at length entirely bony.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: select experimental animals whose anatomical scale and maturity approximate the human condition being modelled. Avoid relying on very young/small animals (dogs, calves) when the clinical target is adult humans because arterial size and bleeding behaviour scale with bulk and age; explicitly consider fetal, adult, and aged differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of biased animal-selection by promoters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Trials of styptics on the bodies of quadrupeds have been commonly practised, to recommend them to the public; but it is not without cause that pretenders to such remedies have made choice of younger animals, as dogs and calves, &c. for that purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern warning: practitioners with commercial or promotional motives may choose younger/smaller animals to make a remedy appear effective. Scrutinize species/age choices and consider whether they systematically bias results toward apparent efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate both immediate haemostasis and subsequent tissue damage/adverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations that although the powder stopped bleeding, human patients experienced “intolerable pains” and stumps resembled actual cautery with “large eschars, and so horrid an appearance,” proving the powder to be a “violent caustic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome assessment should include short-term effects (stopping haemorrhage) and longer-term local tissue responses (pain, eschar formation, necrosis). Do not judge a treatment successful solely on immediate haemostasis without documenting subsequent suffering or tissue injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical application and procedural reporting detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of attempts: multiple successless applications, insertion of a small tent dipped in the powder into the extremity of the bleeding artery, subsequent re-bleeding hours later, and application of a strict bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting standard: describe number of attempts, precise technique (e.g., insertion of a tent into artery), timing of interventions and re-bleeding, bandaging method, and post-operative course. Such procedural detail is necessary to evaluate reproducibility and cause of failure or harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experimental placement to avoid local environmental bias
rubrics_metrics.description: For rain-gauging: the tunnel “was so placed, that there was no building near it that would give occasion to suspect that it did not receive its due proportion of rain,” and the inlet was about 9 yards perpendicularly above the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental setup must avoid nearby obstructions or structures that could bias sampling. Specify placement (height, exposure) so the collected sample truly represents ambient conditions and is comparable to other sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify instrument dimensions, calibration, and conversion factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed specification: a round tunnel of 12 inches diameter fixed to a leaden pipe; a cylindrical glass calibrated to contain just a pound (12 ounces Troy) and marked for smaller parts; weight-based gauging grounded on 22.7368 cubic inches of rain-water per pound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement reporting should include physical dimensions of collectors, calibration marks, and the constants/conversions used. Provide the conversion factors and show how volumes/weights map to heights so others can reproduce and convert results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred measurement method to minimize cumulative error (weight-based filling-to-pound method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than recording the rain that falls between observations (which may accumulate large errors), the author fills a cylindrical glass to the pound mark, throws away full pounds, and records pounds thrown away plus fractional parts remaining to compute totals between times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data-collection protocol: sample repeatedly (twice or thrice daily), use a calibrated receiver, fill to an invariant unit (pound) to avoid summation error, and record both whole units discarded and fractional remnants. This reduces per-interval rounding errors and simplifies aggregation over long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record concurrent meteorological observations
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring rain the author notes taking several other observations, “both of the thermometer, barometer, winds, &c.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual data: routinely record temperature, barometric pressure, wind, and other environmental variables alongside precipitation measurements to aid interpretation and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and quantify measurement accuracy and provide corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: The author states the method’s numbers give heights “so near the truth, that they only fall short of it 1 inch in 200” and recommends adding “3.10, its 200th part” for the true height; later gives mean values and how sums correspond to heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit error estimates and practical corrections to reported quantities. State expected magnitude of measurement error, demonstrate how to correct for systematic biases, and report mean values with their derivation so readers can assess precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare and harmonize instrument standards between sites
rubrics_metrics.description: P.S. remark: there is a “great harmony” between mercurial standards at London and Townley; simultaneous observations show the mercury rose/fell at same times though levels differed by a small amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, compare local instrument readings against recognized standards or neighboring stations to check consistency. Note and report systematic offsets to enable calibration and comparability across sites.
